claims.text: The degree and spatial distribution of local chemical order govern dislocation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Local chemical order governs macroscopic strength and deformation response.
Lower homogenization-annealing temperatures produce greater local chemical order than high-temperature annealing.
Local chemical order creates a rugged energy landscape for moving dislocations through spatially variable stacking-fault, twin-boundary, and antiphase-boundary energies.
Local chemical order activates nanoscale segment-detrapping processes that increase resistance to deformation.
Equiatomic NiCoCr is an FCC medium-entropy alloy that can be treated as a single-phase concentrated solid solution.
The local chemical order in NiCoCr can be tuned through homogenization-annealing temperature.
At sufficiently low mechanical-test temperatures, the local chemical order established during annealing remains effectively frozen during deformation.
High-temperature annealing minimizes local chemical order and approximates a random solid solution.
Pairwise short-range-order parameters quantify the magnitude and spatial distribution of local chemical order.
At lower homogenization temperatures, enthalpic interactions among the principal elements become more important and promote chemical ordering.
Greater local chemical order increases the spatial variability of stacking-fault, twin-boundary, and local antiphase-boundary energies.
Spatial variation in defect energies affects dislocation nucleation and motion.
Nanoscale segment-detrapping processes are involved in the strength-controlling dislocation behavior of concentrated alloys.
Lower-temperature-annealed samples will have higher yield strength than higher-temperature-annealed samples.
Changing local chemical order will alter dislocation slip paths and the activation of nanoscale segment-detrapping processes.
Lower-temperature-annealed samples will exhibit altered ductility relative to samples with minimal local chemical order.
A high-temperature-annealed random-solid-solution baseline has lower lattice resistance to dislocation motion.
The proposed mechanism is expected mainly when local chemical order dominates defect energies and may fail when atomic-size mismatch or other microstructural defects dominate.
